output.title: Time Management Training and Student Stress

scenes.narration: This paper asks whether a short time management training can lower undergraduate students’ perceived stress and raise their perceived control of time.
scenes.layout_description: A central student sits between a tangled clock and a calmer highlighted schedule.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw one student at a desk, with a messy clock cloud on one side and an orderly calendar on the other, orange arrow pointing toward calm planning.

scenes.narration: The authors begin from concern that university students often report stress, and that time-related demands are a serious problem for many students.
scenes.layout_description: A worried student is surrounded by floating clocks, books, and assignment sheets.
scenes.visual_prompt: Illustrate a student holding their head, encircled by simple clock faces and papers, with orange stress lines around the head.

scenes.narration: They note that earlier studies linked student stress with workload, time pressure, self-organized learning, examinations, social integration, habits, and financial concerns too.
scenes.layout_description: Small labeled icons form a ring around one student figure.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw one student in the center with simple icons around them: books, clock, exam paper, people, bed and plate, wallet, all connected by thin lines.

scenes.narration: Time management is presented as a coping strategy, but the authors say intervention research on training effectiveness for students remains scarce overall.
scenes.layout_description: A small toolbox marked with a clock sits beside a mostly empty evidence shelf.
scenes.visual_prompt: Show a hand opening a toolbox with a clock and checklist inside, next to a sparse shelf with only a few paper sheets highlighted in yellow.

scenes.narration: Their research question was whether training could increase perceived control of time and reduce perceived stress, measured here with the tension scale.
scenes.layout_description: Two outcome arrows point from a training board to a calmer student and a stronger clock grip.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw a training flip chart sending orange arrows toward a relaxed student and a hand holding a clock, with a small meter labeled tension.

scenes.narration: They also expected perceived, self-reported demands to remain unchanged, because the training was not designed to change external demands students faced directly.
scenes.layout_description: A steady stack of tasks sits outside the student while internal stress lines fade.
scenes.visual_prompt: Illustrate a student beside an unchanged pile of books and duties, with an orange bracket showing the pile stays the same while the student looks steadier.

scenes.narration: The design trained one group, then compared variables that should change with a control variable from the same stress-related domain of measures.
scenes.layout_description: One group of students splits into two measurement paths, one changing and one steady.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw a single group of students under a training sign, then two arrows leading to a rising control-of-time line and a flat demands line.

scenes.narration: This was called a non-equivalent dependent variable design, also described as an internal referencing strategy in the paper’s Design section by name.
scenes.layout_description: A design diagram compares three gauges before and after training.
scenes.visual_prompt: Show a simple before-and-after chart with three gauges: tension, time control, and demands, with the demands gauge staying still.

scenes.narration: Forty-eight local undergraduate students attended, but the main analyses used the 23 participants who completed all three questionnaires across the study period.
scenes.layout_description: A larger group narrows to a smaller highlighted group holding three forms.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw 48 small dots loosely grouped, with an orange funnel narrowing to 23 larger student figures each holding three questionnaire sheets.

scenes.narration: These 23 students had a mean age of 23.30 years, and about half of the participants were female, 52 %, in this sample.
scenes.layout_description: A small sample portrait shows simple student faces with two exact numbers beside them.
scenes.visual_prompt: Illustrate a row of simple student faces, with a highlighted age tag reading 23.30 and a balanced group marker reading 52 % female.

scenes.narration: Students came from different subjects, including psychology, medicine, biology, pedagogy, physics, law, and computer science, and from different semesters of study time.
scenes.layout_description: Seven study icons and a semester ladder surround the sample group.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw a student group with small icons: brain, medical cross, leaf, book, atom, scales, computer, plus a simple ascending semester ladder.

scenes.narration: Most reported no or little experience using time management strategies before training; others reported moderate or some more experience with them already.
scenes.layout_description: A short experience scale shows most marks near the low end.
scenes.visual_prompt: Illustrate a horizontal experience scale from empty to full, with most orange dots clustered near the low end and a few near the middle.

scenes.narration: The training lasted 4 h, took place in the middle of the semester, and was held by one experienced trainer, in groups.
scenes.layout_description: A trainer stands at a board with a small student group and a clock.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw one trainer pointing to a board, a small seated student group, and a clock highlighted with 4 h above a semester timeline.

scenes.narration: It focused on prioritizing, goal setting, strategy development, daily planning, and monitoring, drawn from Häfner and Stock’s earlier training work in 2010.
scenes.layout_description: Five simple training cards are arranged in a neat row.
scenes.visual_prompt: Show five hand-drawn cards with icons: star priority, target goal, stepping stones, daily calendar, checklist, linked by orange arrows.

scenes.narration: First, students reflected on academic and extracurricular activities, asked which mattered most, and connected important activities with their study goals in writing.
scenes.layout_description: A student sorts activity notes into an important pile leading to a goal flag.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw a student moving sticky notes from a mixed pile into a highlighted important pile, with an arrow to a flag labeled study goals.

scenes.narration: Next, they defined concrete, challenging, proximal goals with deadlines, then planned steps, priorities, starts, obstacles, and possible ways around obstacles for action.
scenes.layout_description: A path of steps leads around a rock toward a deadline flag.
scenes.visual_prompt: Illustrate a path with stepping stones, priority stars, a starting arrow, a rock obstacle, and a curved orange route toward a flag with a clock.

scenes.narration: Daily planning asked what to do, when and where to do it, how much time to schedule, and how to avoid distractions.
scenes.layout_description: A day planner page has time blocks and a crossed-out distraction symbol.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw an open planner with simple time blocks, a location pin, a small hourglass, and a phone-like distraction crossed out in orange.

scenes.narration: The final part asked trainees to monitor tasks each day, seeing what was completed and what still had to be done next.
scenes.layout_description: A checklist shows completed items and remaining items under a watchful eye.
scenes.visual_prompt: Illustrate a checklist with several orange check marks, a few empty boxes, and a simple eye icon above it for monitoring.

scenes.narration: Measurements were taken directly before training, 2 weeks after training, and 4 weeks after training, within the same external context of semester.
scenes.layout_description: A three-point timeline runs left to right with a constant semester frame around it.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw a horizontal timeline with three marked dots: before, 2 weeks, 4 weeks, all inside one large bracket labeled semester.

scenes.narration: Time management behaviour was measured with 18 items about behaviours such as prioritizing, setting clear goals, and monitoring, rated by participants themselves.
scenes.layout_description: A questionnaire sheet shows small boxes beside planning icons.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw a questionnaire page with 18 tiny check boxes suggested by grouped marks, plus icons for star priority, target, and checklist.

scenes.narration: Tension used five items about mental fatigue, trouble relaxing, and nervousness; perceived control of time used ten adapted items from prior work.
scenes.layout_description: Two measurement cards sit side by side, one showing strain and one showing clock control.
scenes.visual_prompt: Illustrate two cards: one with a tired face and wavy stress lines, the other with a hand steadying a clock, each with small item boxes.

scenes.narration: Demands used five items about work amount and external duties, serving as the variable expected not to change after training in analyses.
scenes.layout_description: A task pile is measured before and after with the same height.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw two identical stacks of books and duty papers on a simple scale, before and after, connected by a flat yellow line.

scenes.narration: After training, reported use of time management strategies increased significantly by 4 weeks, and was nearly significant after 2 weeks as reported.
scenes.layout_description: A line graph rises from before to 4 weeks, with the middle point softly highlighted.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw a simple upward line with three dots; the 2-week dot is lightly circled yellow, and the 4-week dot is strongly circled orange.

scenes.narration: Two weeks after training, trainees reported significantly less stress on tension; perceived control of time showed a tendency in the expected direction.
scenes.layout_description: The tension gauge drops, while the control gauge nudges upward without a strong mark.
scenes.visual_prompt: Illustrate two gauges: tension needle clearly lower with an orange check, time control needle slightly higher with a small dotted arrow.

scenes.narration: Four weeks after training, trainees reported significantly less stress and significantly more perceived control of time than directly before training at pretest.
scenes.layout_description: Two strong arrows show stress down and time control up at the final measurement.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw a calm student holding a planner, with a bold downward arrow on a tension gauge and upward arrow on a clock-control gauge.

scenes.narration: Demands did not change significantly at 2 or 4 weeks, supporting the authors’ conclusion that effects were attributable to training rather specifically.
scenes.layout_description: A flat demands line contrasts with changing stress and control lines.
scenes.visual_prompt: Show three simple lines: demands flat, tension down, time control up, with the flat line highlighted to show the control comparison.

scenes.narration: The authors call this preliminary because of the small sample and dropout, and say larger intervention studies are necessary for robust conclusions.
scenes.layout_description: A small paper sits beside a larger blank future study board.
scenes.visual_prompt: Draw a small completed study sheet with 23 dots beside a larger empty research board, with an orange arrow pointing toward future studies.
